newsitem.title: UK: Inflation rise puts pressure on British government.
newsitem.headline: Inflation rise puts pressure on British government.

text.p: British inflation jumped to its highest level in three years in October, official data showed Thursday, putting the government under increased pressure to raise interest rates again.
Retail prices rose by 2.7 percent in the year to October, compared with 2.1 percent in September, the Office for National Statistics said.
The politically important underlying rate, which excludes mortage interest payments, climbed to 3.3 percent from 2.9 percent in September.
That marked its highest rate in more than three years and well above the government's 2.5 percent target.
Economists said the figures were bad news.
"The figures are really quite bad ... showing that retailers are now quite confident about putting up prices," Ciaran Barr, an economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said.
"It puts the inflation target in extreme jeopardy and is very negative for (financial) markets."
Economists said calls for higher interest rates from the Bank of England and some independent analysts were now likely to grow louder.
The government, however, shrugged off the news.
"Policy is set to meet our inflation target. That is why we are sustaining our best inflation record in 50 years," Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said in a statement.
He said technical reasons were behind the large yearly jump in prices. The month-on-month change in both underlying and headline inflation was nil, he said.
The opposition Labour Party, however, pounced on the figures as evidence the government has mismanaged the economy.
"The Tories cannot be trusted on the economy. We are not best in Europe for inflation, but 11th out of 15," said Labour finance spokesman Gordon Brown.
"Within two months of declaring an economic miracle, the cracks are already appearing. Today's news makes a mockery of the Prime Minister's (John Major) claim that he had conquered inflation."
